warmup.q: An NIO server registers every connection for OP_READ | OP_WRITE so it can write "whenever it needs to". One client connects and sends nothing. What does the server's loop do for the next second?
options: Sleeps in select() until the client sends something
Wakes once, sees nothing to write, and goes back to sleep
Wakes up again and again, hundreds of thousands of times, because the socket is always writable
warmup.why: A socket with free space in its send buffer is writable, and Linux selectors are level-triggered, so every select() reports that idle connection again at once. The demo in this lesson counted 0 wakeups with OP_READ alone and 431,909 in 300 ms with OP_WRITE added.

sections.h: A ByteBuffer is a cursor with two marks
sections.html:
Everything in java.nio moves bytes through a ByteBuffer: a fixed block of memory with three numbers. capacity is its size. position is where the next put or get happens. limit is where reading or writing must stop. Most NIO bugs are one of these three numbers being wrong.

A fresh buffer is in write mode: position 0 and limit equal to capacity. Each put moves position forward. Before you can read what you wrote, flip() sets limit to the current position and position back to 0. This section's demo walks a 16-byte buffer through the whole cycle:

allocate(16)         pos=0  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=16
put("hello")         pos=5  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11
flip()               pos=0  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=5
get(2) -> "he"       pos=2  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=3
compact()            pos=3  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=13
put("XY")            pos=5  lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11
flip()               pos=0  lim=5  cap=16 remaining=5
readable content: "lloXY"

compact() is the call server code needs most. It copies the unread bytes (llo) to the front and puts the buffer back in write mode right after them, so new data lands behind what you haven't used yet. clear() looks similar and does something else: it resets both marks and forgets everything, read or not.

Forget flip() and nothing throws. A buffer of 8 with 2 bytes put has remaining() 6, so a write sends the 6 bytes after your data, whatever they happen to be.

There are two kinds of buffer. allocate gives a heap buffer backed by a byte[]. allocateDirect gives memory outside the Java heap. The JDK's Javadoc says direct buffers have "somewhat higher allocation and deallocation costs" and recommends them for large, long-lived buffers used for native IO. They exist because the kernel reads and writes memory by address during a system call, and the garbage collector is allowed to move a byte[] on the heap. So the JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read and write (sun.nio.ch.IOUtil does it). So allocate direct buffers once and reuse them. Netty's pooled allocators do exactly that for you.

sections.h: Non-blocking reads and writes move only what fits
sections.html:
Every TCP socket has two buffers inside the kernel. The receive buffer holds bytes that arrived from the network and that your program hasn't read yet. The send buffer holds bytes your program wrote that the kernel hasn't delivered to the other side yet. read and write never touch the network themselves: they copy between your ByteBuffer and these kernel buffers.

Put a SocketChannel in non-blocking mode with configureBlocking(false) and those copies stop waiting. They do what the buffers allow right now and return.

read(buf) copies whatever sits in the socket's receive buffer. That can be one byte, half a message, three messages, or nothing at all, in which case it returns 0. It returns -1 when the other side has closed its end. write(buf) is the call that bites. Its Javadoc says a socket channel in non-blocking mode "cannot write any more bytes than are free in the socket's output buffer". When the client reads slowly, the kernel's send buffer fills, and write sends part of your buffer or none of it.

So every connection needs its own buffer for the bytes it hasn't sent yet. The pattern that handles both directions is four lines:

Java
int n = ch.read(buf);    // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done
buf.flip();              // switch to reading what we hold
ch.write(buf);           // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it
buf.compact();           // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode
Kotlin
val n = ch.read(buf)     // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done
buf.flip()               // switch to reading what we hold
ch.write(buf)            // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it
buf.compact()            // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode

After compact(), buf.position() > 0 means bytes are still waiting. One run for this track echoed 8 MiB to a client with a 4 KiB receive buffer and counted 8 partial writes. With clear() in place of compact(), each of them would have dropped bytes.

The read side has a twin rule: one read is not one message. TCP is a byte stream. A payment message sent with one write can arrive in three reads, and two messages can arrive in one. Anything more than raw echo needs framing, such as a length prefix or a delimiter. Lesson 4 builds one with Netty.

One trap lives in the client. If a test client writes 8 MiB and only then starts reading, the echo stalls: the server can't send because the client isn't reading, so the server stops reading, so the client's write blocks. Clients of an echo server must read and write at the same time. The lab's tests use a writer thread for exactly this reason.

sections.h: A Selector tells one thread which channels are ready
sections.html:
A Selector watches many channels at once. You register each channel with an interest set, the operations you care about (OP_ACCEPT, OP_READ, OP_WRITE), and select() blocks until at least one of them is ready. Each registration is a SelectionKey. It carries the interest set, the ready set that the selector fills in, and an attachment where you keep that connection's state.

Java
while (true) {
    selector.select();                                  // sleep until something is ready
    Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator();
    while (it.hasNext()) {
        SelectionKey key = it.next();
        it.remove();                                    // you must remove handled keys yourself
        if (key.isAcceptable()) {
            SocketChannel ch = server.accept();
            ch.configureBlocking(false);
            ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, new Conn());
        } else {
            serve(key);                                 // read, write, update the interest set
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
while (true) {
    selector.select()                                   // sleep until something is ready
    val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator()
    while (it.hasNext()) {
        val key = it.next()
        it.remove()                                     // you must remove handled keys yourself
        if (key.isAcceptable) {
            val ch = server.accept()
            ch.configureBlocking(false)
            ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, Conn())
        } else {
            serve(key)                                  // read, write, update the interest set
        }
    }
}

The it.remove() line is not optional. The selector adds keys to the selected-key set and never takes them out. Leave a key in and the next pass handles it again with its old ready set. In this section's demo, one 6-byte message was handled as readable 7 times in 300 ms. For an accept key, that means calling accept() again and getting null back.

The selector also comes with a threading rule. Its Javadoc says a selector is safe for concurrent use, but its selected-key set is not. The simple way to obey that is the one every framework uses: one thread owns a selector, runs its loop, and does all the work for its channels. Netty calls that thread an event loop.

On Linux, Selector.open() returns sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl, a wrapper around epoll. On macOS you get a kqueue selector. The JDK registers sockets with epoll in level-triggered mode: as long as a socket is readable or writable, every select() reports it again. That one fact is behind the bug in the next section.

try.title: Forget it.remove()
steps: Open StaleKeyDemo.java (or StaleKeyDemo.kt). A client sends exactly one 6-byte message, and the loop runs for 300 ms, once removing handled keys and once not.
Predict how many times each version treats the channel as readable.
Run it with the command below.

code.title: StaleKeyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; import java.util.Iterator; /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ public class StaleKeyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(true); run(false); } static void run(boolean removeHandledKeys) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ); client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth-1".getBytes())); // exactly one message ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64); int loops = 0, handled = 0, bytes = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50); loops++; Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove(); if (key.isReadable()) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++; buf.clear(); bytes += Math.max(0, conn.read(buf)); } } } System.out.printf("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d%n", removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes); } } } }

How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ fun main() { staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = true) staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = false) } private fun staleKeys(removeHandledKeys: Boolean) { Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { client -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ) client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth-1".toByteArray())) // exactly one message val buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64) var loops = 0 var handled = 0 var bytes = 0 val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50) loops++ val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove() if (key.isReadable) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++ buf.clear() bytes += maxOf(0, conn.read(buf)) } } } println("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d" .format(removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes)) } } } } }

try.expect: With it.remove(): handled once, 6 bytes read. Without it: handled 7 times in 7 loop passes, still 6 bytes in total. The six extra passes each called read and got 0 bytes back, because the key stayed in the selected set and isReadable() kept returning true from the old ready set.

sections.h: Arm OP_WRITE only while bytes are waiting
sections.html:
A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has free space, which is nearly always. Combine that with level-triggered epoll and you get the classic NIO bug. Register OP_WRITE on every connection and select() never sleeps again: it returns at once, reports every idle connection as writable, and the loop goes around again.

This section's demo measures it on one idle connection for 300 ms:

Selector implementation: sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl
idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ           : 0 wakeups
idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: 431909 wakeups

Zero against several hundred thousand, on a connection that sent nothing. Under strace the shape is just as clear: thousands of epoll_wait calls and a handful of epoll_ctl. In production it looks like a server at 100% of one core with no traffic.

The rule is to register OP_READ by default and add OP_WRITE only while the connection has unsent bytes. When a write leaves bytes behind, arm it. When a later write drains them, drop it:

Java
boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0;   // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front
int ops = 0;
if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ;   // room left: keep reading
if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE;                                // only while bytes wait
key.interestOps(ops);
Kotlin
val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0        // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front
var ops = 0
if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ   // room left: keep reading
if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE                                // only while bytes wait
key.interestOps(ops)

The OP_READ line is the other half of the same idea. When the buffer is full because the client reads slowly, stop reading from that client. Its bytes pile up in your socket's receive buffer, and TCP tells the client how much free space is left there (the TCP window). As the window shrinks to zero, the client's own writes stop. That is backpressure in two lines, and lesson 4 shows Netty's version of it: writability and AUTO_READ. In the 8 MiB run mentioned earlier, the server armed OP_WRITE only 4 times in 537 selects.

Closing follows the same logic. A client can half-close a connection (shutdownOutput()): it says it will send nothing more but keeps reading. Your read then returns -1, yet the client still wants the rest of its echo. Close only once nothing is pending.

code.title: SpinDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ public class SpinDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (Selector probe = Selector.open()) { System.out.println("Selector implementation: " + probe.getClass().getName()); } System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ) + " wakeups"); System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ | SelectionKey.OP_WRITE) + " wakeups"); } static long wakeups(int interest) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, interest); long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L, count = 0; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++; // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear(); } return count; } } } }

alt.html: package workbench.nio.l02 import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey import java.nio.channels.Selector import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ fun main() { Selector.open().use { println("Selector implementation: ${it.javaClass.name}") } println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ)} wakeups") println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE)} wakeups") } private fun idleWakeups(interest: Int): Long = Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { _ -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, interest) val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L var count = 0L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++ // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear() } count } } } }

try.expect: 0 wakeups with OP_READ, and hundreds of thousands with OP_WRITE added (431,909 and 534,481 in two runs on my 4-core Linux machine; the exact number depends on CPU speed). Under strace the loop slows down a lot, because strace stops the process on every system call, but the table still shows thousands of epoll_wait calls (4,315 in my run) against 5 epoll_ctl. On macOS the first line names the kqueue selector.

analogy: Level-triggered readiness is a doorbell that rings for as long as someone stands at the door. OP_READ asks "ring while a visitor is waiting": you answer, take the parcel, and it stops. OP_WRITE asks "ring while there is room in the outbox", and the outbox is nearly always empty, so it rings all day and you keep walking to the door for nothing. Ask for that ring only when you have a letter to post. The analogy breaks in one place: epoll doesn't ring on its own. Your loop asks it, and level-triggered means it answers yes every time you ask.
world: You won't write raw selectors in a Quarkus service, but you will debug their failure modes. A Vert.x or Netty process at 100% of one core with no traffic is often a loop that wakes without work to do. Netty itself fixed one in 4.2.20 (commit 06518dc): a timer due in under half a millisecond rounded the select timeout down to 0, so a loop with a pending timer polled the selector in a circle. Partial reads matter every time you parse a TCP protocol by hand, such as an ISO 8583 link to a card network: a message arrives in several reads, and only its length prefix tells you when you have all of it.
mistake: The classic mistake is registering OP_WRITE together with OP_READ "so the loop can write whenever it needs to". On a level-triggered selector a socket with buffer space is always writable, so the loop spins at 100% CPU. The second classic is assuming one write sends the whole buffer and calling clear() after it, which silently drops bytes as soon as a client reads slowly. Write, compact(), check position() > 0, and arm OP_WRITE only then. Close on EOF only after the pending bytes are gone.

compare.title: The serve step in Java and Kotlin

java.title: serve, Java
java.html: private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); }

kotlin.title: serve, Kotlin
kotlin.html: private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) }

compare.note: Both call the same JDK API, so behavior is identical: same partial writes, same level-triggered selector. The differences are surface ones that still trip people up. Kotlin has no |= for bit flags, so you write ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ. Kotlin reads isReadable() and isAcceptable() as properties (key.isReadable), and the attachment is an untyped Any? that you cast with as Conn, just as Java casts from Object. Neither language helps you with the buffer's mode: flip() and compact() are runtime state, not types, so the compiler can't stop you from writing a buffer that is still in write mode.

worked.title: Trace one connection through a partial write

steps.say: The client sends 20 KiB and reads slowly. The server's buffer holds 16 KiB. First select(): readable. The server reads 16 KiB, flips, and the kernel accepts only 6 KiB of the write.
steps.code:
read 16384      -> pos=16384 lim=16384   (buffer full)
flip()          -> pos=0     lim=16384
write -> 6144   -> pos=6144  lim=16384   (10240 bytes not sent)
compact()       -> pos=10240 lim=16384   (pending: 10240, room: 6144)
interest        =  OP_READ | OP_WRITE

steps.say: Second select(): readable (the other 4 KiB arrived) and writable (the client read some). The server appends 4 KiB behind the pending bytes, then sends everything it holds.
steps.code:
read 4096       -> pos=14336 lim=16384
flip()          -> pos=0     lim=14336
write -> 14336  -> pos=14336 lim=14336   (all sent)
compact()       -> pos=0     lim=16384   (pending: 0)
interest        =  OP_READ               (OP_WRITE dropped: nothing to send)

steps.say: Now the client half-closes while the server still holds bytes. read returns -1, so stop reading, but keep OP_WRITE until the tail is gone. Close in the pass where pending reaches zero.
steps.code: // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } key.interestOps((conn.eof ? 0 : SelectionKey.OP_READ) | (pending ? SelectionKey.OP_WRITE : 0));

alt.html: // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } key.interestOps((if (conn.eof) 0 else SelectionKey.OP_READ) or (if (pending) SelectionKey.OP_WRITE else 0))

steps.say: The lab's version adds one more condition: drop OP_READ while the buffer has no room left. Without it, a full buffer and a readable socket make the same spin as a stray OP_WRITE: select() says readable, read() copies 0 bytes into the full buffer, and the loop goes around again.

lab.title: Fix an NIO echo server that loses bytes and burns a core
steps: Run the tests. All three fail: the 4 MiB echo comes back short, the half-close test loses its tail, and an idle connection wakes the selector hundreds of thousands of times.
In accept(), register the new channel for OP_READ only.
In serve(), replace clear() with compact() so unsent bytes stay at the front, and only call write when the flipped buffer hasRemaining().
Close the channel only when conn.eof is true and nothing is pending (buf.position() == 0 after compact()).
End serve() by setting the interest set: OP_READ while not at EOF and the buffer has room, OP_WRITE only while bytes are pending. Run the tests three times.
hints: After compact(), position() is exactly the number of bytes still waiting to be sent.
The tests give the client a 4 KiB receive buffer, and the server's sockets an 8 KiB send buffer, so partial writes happen early and often. Your code must not depend on those sizes.
If idleConnectionDoesNotSpin still fails, look for any path through serve() that returns with OP_WRITE still set after the buffer drained.
The half-close test reads slowly on purpose. If it fails with a few kilobytes missing, you close on EOF before the pending bytes are written.
lab.done: All three tests in NioEchoServerTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the serve step from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write serve(SelectionKey key) for an echo server whose per-connection state is a ByteBuffer buf and a boolean eof: read, flip, write, compact, close on EOF only when drained, and set the interest ops. Then check: which line stops the busy spin, and which one applies backpressure?

answer.html: private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); } // busy spin: OP_WRITE only if pending // backpressure: OP_READ only if the buffer has room

alt.html: private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) } // busy spin: OP_WRITE only if pending // backpressure: OP_READ only if the buffer has room

recap: A ByteBuffer has position, limit and capacity. flip() switches to reading, compact() keeps unread bytes and switches back, clear() forgets everything.
Non-blocking read returns what is there (maybe 0, or -1 at EOF), and write may send only part of the buffer. Keep unsent bytes per connection.
One read is not one message. Frame your protocol with a length prefix or a delimiter.
Remove every handled key from selectedKeys(). One thread owns a selector and does all the work for its channels.
Linux selectors are level-triggered epoll, so OP_WRITE on an idle socket fires forever. Arm it only while bytes are pending, drop OP_READ while your buffer is full, and close only when drained.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why an NIO echo server must not keep OP_WRITE registered all the time, and what it should do after a write that sent only part of its buffer.
explain.answer: On Linux the selector is level-triggered: it reports a channel as long as the condition holds. A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has space, which is almost always, so a permanent OP_WRITE makes every select() return immediately and the loop burns a core doing nothing. After a partial write, the server should keep the unsent bytes (call compact() so they move to the front), register OP_WRITE so the selector says when the socket can take more, and go back to select() to serve other connections. When a later write drains the buffer, it removes OP_WRITE again. While the buffer is full it should also drop OP_READ, which pushes back on a client that sends faster than it reads.

deeper.html:
Level-triggered and edge-triggered are the two ways epoll can report readiness. Level-triggered, the default, reports a socket on every epoll_wait for as long as it is readable or writable. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET) reports it once, when it changes from not ready to ready, and then stays quiet until the next change. The JDK's EPollSelectorImpl never sets EPOLLET, so Selector is level-triggered on Linux. That is forgiving for reads (if you leave bytes unread, the next select() tells you again) and unforgiving for OP_WRITE.

Edge-triggered code has the opposite trap: after a notification you must read until read returns 0, or you never hear about the leftover bytes. The JDK's virtual-thread poller, which lesson 8 looks at, uses a third mode, EPOLLONESHOT: report once, then disarm until the fd is registered again. That fits its job, which is to wake one parked thread once.

Two more details from the JDK source. EPollSelectorImpl asks epoll_wait for at most min(fdLimit, 1024) events per call, so a selector with 10,000 ready sockets needs several calls to see them all. And Netty's NIO transport still carries a guard against selectors that return early with nothing selected: after 512 such returns in a row (io.netty.selectorAutoRebuildThreshold), it rebuilds the selector. That is the old "epoll spin bug" workaround, and the reason NioIoHandler counts empty wakeups.

To see the system calls yourself on Linux, run any demo that only uses JDK classes outside Gradle with strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo <class>. -c prints a count per system call when the process exits.
